# Summary {.unnumbered}

Walker asks Bayesians to think of a prior as one probability measure on a space
of possible sampling distributions. A parametric prior is concentrated on a
fixed finite-dimensional family; a Bayesian nonparametric prior is not confined
to one such family. Conditional iid sampling from a random
distribution produces an exchangeable sequence, Bayes' rule updates the law of
that distribution, and the posterior predictive averages candidate sampling
distributions under the posterior.

The chapter then makes three less elementary moves:

1. use decision theory to project a rich posterior onto a simpler parametric
   action;
2. evaluate whether the posterior learning rule is consistent when data really
   arise iid from a fixed $f_0$;
3. derive the ordinary posterior—and fractional alternatives—by minimizing
   expected log loss plus KL divergence from the prior.

Some of Walker's statements about “complete” priors, model selection, and
coherence are forcefully argued philosophical positions. This note labels them
as such rather than presenting them as consequences of measure theory.

# Walker fast path {.unnumbered #walker-fast-path}

This reconstruction assumes the probability, likelihood, posterior, and
regression-level asymptotics normally used in graduate biostatistics. It does
not assume measure theory, real analysis, topology, stochastic-process theory,
or functional analysis.

You can begin with this note. The broader companion notes are reference notes,
not required cover-to-cover reading. This page repeats every idea needed for
the chapter and sends you to a **specific section** only when a fuller
explanation would help.

still unfamiliar:

# 1. Put every object on its correct space {#walker-object-spaces}

**Optional companion excerpt.** Read
[The two measurable spaces](../Measure_Theory/random-probability-measures.qmd#rpm-two-spaces)
to see how data-space events and sets of candidate distributions form two
different measurable spaces. Read
[A prior on densities](bayes-measure-d-concept.qmd#notation-prior-on-densities)
only if the type of object measured by $\Pi$ is still unclear.

Let

- $(\mathcal X,\mathscr X)$ be the observation space;
- $\lambda$ be a common dominating measure on that space;
- $\mathcal D$ be a collection of candidate densities relative to $\lambda$;
- $\mathscr G$ be a sigma-field on $\mathcal D$;
- $\Pi$ be a probability measure on $(\mathcal D,\mathscr G)$.

A useful symbol map is

| Symbol | Type | Role |
|---|---|---|
| $x$ | Point in $\mathcal X$ | A possible observation |
| $f$ | Point in $\mathcal D$ | An entire candidate density |
| $P_f$ | Probability measure on $\mathcal X$ | Sampling distribution with $dP_f/d\lambda=f$ |
| $\Pi$ | Probability measure on $\mathcal D$ | Prior law of the random density |
| $\Pi_n$ | Probability measure on $\mathcal D$ | Posterior law after $n$ observations |
| $P_n^{\mathrm{pred}}$ | Probability measure on $\mathcal X$ | Posterior predictive distribution |
| $f_0$ | Fixed density | True data-generating density in the asymptotic analysis |

This table prevents the most common confusion: $P_f$ and $\Pi$ are both
probability measures, but they act on different spaces.

The sigma-field $\mathscr G$ is the collection of subsets of the density space
to which $\Pi$ may assign prior probability. Its members are sets of entire
density functions, not sets of observed $x$ values.

Walker works with densities. In other BNP models the random object may instead
be a probability measure $G$, a distribution function, a regression function,
or a hazard. Then use $\Pi(dG)$ or the corresponding notation.

# 2. The random-distribution model {#walker-random-model}

**Optional companion excerpt.**
[A random probability measure](../Measure_Theory/random-probability-measures.qmd#rpm-definition)
develops the same hierarchy with a general distribution $G$ rather than only
a density $f$. It explains the source of randomness behind the phrase
“random distribution.”

The basic hierarchy is

$$
f\sim\Pi,
\qquad
X_i\mid f\overset{\mathrm{iid}}\sim P_f.
\tag{1}
$$

Operationally:

1. draw one entire density $f$ from the prior law $\Pi$;
2. conditional on that $f$, draw all observations iid from $P_f$.

The density is shared across observations. This sharing is what makes one
observation informative about the distribution of another.

## Conditional independence versus marginal dependence

Conditional on $f$,

$$
P(X_1\in A_1,\ldots,X_n\in A_n\mid f)
=\prod_{i=1}^nP_f(A_i).
$$

After integrating out $f$,

$$
P(X_1\in A_1,\ldots,X_n\in A_n)
=\int_{\mathcal D}
\prod_{i=1}^nP_f(A_i)\Pi(df).
\tag{2}
$$

The observations are generally dependent marginally because learning about
the shared $f$ couples them.

# 3. Why exchangeability appears {#walker-exchangeability}

**Optional companion excerpt.**
[Connection to exchangeability](../Measure_Theory/random-probability-measures.qmd#rpm-exchangeability)
shows how conditional iid sampling yields exchangeability after the shared
random distribution is integrated out.

A finite sequence is exchangeable if its joint distribution is invariant to a
permutation of labels. The product in (2) is unchanged when the indices are
reordered. Therefore a conditional-iid mixture is exchangeable.

This is true for both parametric and nonparametric Bayesian models. A
parametric hierarchy

$$
\theta\sim\pi,
\qquad
X_i\mid\theta\overset{\mathrm{iid}}\sim P_\theta
$$

is also exchangeable after $\theta$ is integrated out.

Representation theorems of de Finetti and Hewitt-Savage provide a converse
under suitable conditions: an infinitely exchangeable sequence can be
represented as conditionally iid given a random directing probability measure
[@hewitt1955symmetric]. The theorem motivates random probability measures; it
does not say that every finite exchangeable dataset uniquely determines a BNP
prior.

# 4. Bayes' rule on a space of densities {#walker-bayes-density-space}

**Optional companion excerpt.** Read
[Bayes' rule on the function space](bayes-measure-d-concept.qmd#notation-bayes-function-space)
for the finite-candidate analogy and the derivation of $d\Pi_n/d\Pi$. That
section is the targeted remedy if $\Pi(df\mid X)$ still looks like a
calculus derivative.

For observed $x_{1:n}$, define

$$
L_n(f)=\prod_{i=1}^nf(x_i)
$$

and the marginal likelihood

$$
m_n(x_{1:n})
=\int_{\mathcal D}L_n(g)\Pi(dg).
$$

Assume $f\mapsto L_n(f)$ is $\mathscr G$-measurable and
$0<m_n(x_{1:n})<\infty$. For every measurable
$A\subseteq\mathcal D$, the posterior is

$$
\Pi_n(A)
=\Pi(A\mid x_{1:n})
=\frac{\int_A L_n(f)\Pi(df)}
{\int_{\mathcal D}L_n(g)\Pi(dg)}.
\tag{3}
$$

The compact differential notation

$$
\Pi_n(df)
=\Pi(df\mid x_{1:n})
=\frac{L_n(f)\Pi(df)}{m_n(x_{1:n})}
\tag{4}
$$

means

$$
\frac{d\Pi_n}{d\Pi}(f)
=\frac{L_n(f)}{m_n(x_{1:n})}.
\tag{5}
$$

Equation (5) is a Radon-Nikodym derivative: the normalized likelihood is the
posterior density **relative to the prior measure**. No infinite-dimensional
Lebesgue measure or prior density $\pi(f)$ is required.

The [density prerequisite](../Measure_Theory/lebesgue-measure-integration-and-densities.qmd#the-radon-nikodym-derivative-is-a-measure-level-density)
explains this derivative as the function that converts prior integration into
posterior integration. No proof of the Radon-Nikodym theorem is needed here.

# 5. Posterior prediction {#walker-prediction}

**Optional companion excerpt.**
[Prior and posterior predictive distributions](../Measure_Theory/random-probability-measures.qmd#rpm-prediction)
explains why prediction averages the **sampling measures** under the posterior
law rather than substituting a generic posterior mean parameter.

For a future observation,

$$
P(X_{n+1}\in A\mid X_{1:n})
=\int_{\mathcal D}P_f(A)\Pi_n(df).
\tag{6}
$$

If all $P_f$ have densities relative to $\lambda$, the predictive density is

$$
f_n(x)=\int_{\mathcal D}f(x)\Pi_n(df).
\tag{7}
$$

Equation (7) is a posterior mean at each $x$. The measure form (6) is more
general and avoids calling a distribution with atoms a density.

# 6. Why the model is called “nonparametric” {#walker-nonparametric}

**Optional companion excerpt.**
[Parametric Bayes also induces a prior on distributions](../Measure_Theory/random-probability-measures.qmd#rpm-parametric-induced-prior)
isolates the key distinction: both approaches induce laws on distributions,
but their supports have different dimensional structure.

## Parametric model viewed on density space

Suppose $f=f_\theta$ for $\theta\in\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^p$ and
$\theta\sim\pi$. The map $\theta\mapsto f_\theta$ induces a probability law
$\Pi$ on $\mathcal D$, but its support lies within

$$
\{f_\theta:\theta\in\Theta\},
$$

a fixed finite-dimensional subset.

The **support** of a prior is, informally, the collection of possibilities it
does not rule out, including limiting possibilities. The precise
neighborhood-based definition is given in the
[consistency note](../Measure_Theory/posterior-consistency.qmd#prior-support).

## Nonparametric model

In BNP, the unknown distribution or function is not restricted to one fixed
finite-dimensional family. The prior may live on

- probability distributions;
- densities;
- regression functions;
- hazard or cumulative-hazard functions;
- partitions, feature allocations, or other growing structures.

This does not mean “no parameters,” “all possible functions,” or
“assumption-free.” A BNP prior has hyperparameters, support restrictions, and
regularity assumptions. Its effective complexity can grow with the data.

# 7. Walker's argument about Bayesian choices {#walker-choices}

Walker argues that the prior should represent all uncertainty entertained
before seeing the observations. If the analyst suspects that a normal sampling
family may be wrong, his preferred coherent response is to enlarge the prior
before observing data rather than select a different prior after inspecting
the same data [@walker2010bnp].

## The mathematical fact

A parametric prior can be pushed forward to a prior on sampling distributions,
and it assigns probability one to its parametric family. A richer prior can
assign mass outside that family.

## Walker's normative position

Walker calls a prior “complete” when it incorporates all uncertainties he
believes the analyst should acknowledge. He argues that choosing among priors
after inspecting the data and then reporting the selected analysis as if its
prior had been fixed beforehand is incoherent as a representation of personal
belief.

This should not be expanded into the claims that

- every parametric model is incoherent;
- posterior predictive checking is illegitimate;
- every data-adaptive procedure violates probability axioms;
- one BNP prior can literally anticipate every model inadequacy.

A parametric analysis with a genuinely pre-specified prior is internally
Bayesian. Bayesian model averaging can place a prior on a model index before
data. Model checking can reveal scientifically important failures. The precise
problem Walker targets is unmodeled post-data selection followed by an
interpretation that ignores the selection.

## Special case: a normal truth

A flexible prior can include distributions close to normal while retaining
support for skewness, multimodality, or heavy tails. This can reduce
misspecification bias, but flexibility has a price:

- more prior choices;
- potentially slower learning;
- harder computation;
- more difficult interpretation;
- no automatic guarantee that the true distribution lies in the support.

The honest comparison is therefore not “rigid and wrong” versus “flexible and
true,” but a trade-off among support, regularization, data information, and
computational tractability.

# 8. Prior elicitation through functionals

A **functional** is a rule that takes an entire function or distribution as
its input and returns a number or another summary. For fixed $x$, evaluation
$f\mapsto f(x)$ is a functional. “Pointwise” below means that the summary is
considered separately at each value of $x$.

Walker suggests thinking about functions such as

$$
\mu_1(x)=E_\Pi\{f(x)\},
\qquad
\mu_2(x)=E_\Pi\{f(x)^2\}.
$$

when these pointwise expectations are finite. They express a prior mean density
and pointwise second moment. One can use a
parametric prior as an elicitation benchmark; for example,

$$
\mu_1(x)
=\int N(x\mid\theta,\sigma^2)\pi(d\theta,d\sigma).
$$

A nonparametric prior may be centered to share these summaries while allowing
shapes outside the normal family.

Important limitation: arbitrary choices of $\mu_1$ and $\mu_2$ do not, by
themselves, generally determine a unique valid law on density functions.
Walker is describing an elicitation strategy for suitable process models, not
a universal construction theorem.

# 9. Stochastic-process priors {#walker-process-priors}

**Optional companion excerpt.** Read
[A random measure as a stochastic process](../Measure_Theory/random-probability-measures.qmd#rpm-stochastic-process)
for the general set-indexed-process idea. Read
[The Dirichlet process](../Measure_Theory/random-probability-measures.qmd#rpm-dirichlet-process)
only for Walker's concrete random-measure example; the later DP-mixture section
is not needed to understand this part of the chapter.

A random function is commonly built from a stochastic process, whose law is
the prior. Examples include

- Gaussian processes for regression or transformed log densities;
- independent-increment processes for cumulative hazards;
- the Dirichlet process for random probability measures.

A **stochastic process** is a collection of jointly distributed random
variables indexed by a location such as time or $x$. One complete draw supplies
a value at every index and therefore produces an entire random function. Its
**law** is the probability distribution over all such possible functions.

For a Gaussian process, every finite vector of function values has a
multivariate normal distribution. For an independent-increment process,
changes over nonoverlapping intervals are independent. These facts identify
the examples; their construction theory is not needed for Walker's argument.

For

$$
G\sim\operatorname{DP}(\alpha,H),
$$

every finite measurable partition has Dirichlet-distributed random masses
[@ferguson1973dp]. A DP draw $G$ is almost surely discrete. For continuous
density estimation it is therefore commonly used as a mixing distribution:

$$
f_G(x)=\int k(x\mid\theta)G(d\theta).
$$

The induced law of $f_G$ is Walker's prior $\Pi(df)$. See the
[applied DP-mixture bridge](bayes-nonpar-concept-applied.qmd).

# 10. Decision theory under a rich posterior {#walker-decision-theory}

**Optional companion excerpt.**
[Walker's posterior decision problem](../Other/km-divergence.qmd#kl-walker-decision)
derives the KL orientation and posterior-predictive log-score identity used in
this section. The earlier portions of the KL note are only needed if the
definition of KL itself is unfamiliar.

Walker next asks how to select a lower-dimensional parametric approximation
without pretending it is the full state of nature.

Let

- $f$ be the unknown true density, the state of nature;
- $\theta\in\Theta$ be an action;
- $q_\theta$ be the density implied by action $\theta$.

In decision theory, the **state of nature** is the unknown object relevant to
the consequence of a decision; an **action** is what the analyst chooses; a
utility ranks the consequence of choosing that action under a given state.

Choose the KL-based utility

$$
u(f,\theta)
=-D_{\mathrm{KL}}(f\|q_\theta)
=-\int f(x)\log\frac{f(x)}{q_\theta(x)}\lambda(dx).
\tag{8}
$$

The posterior expected utility is

$$
U_n(\theta)
=\int_{\mathcal D}u(f,\theta)\Pi_n(df).
\tag{9}
$$

Expanding (8),

$$
\begin{aligned}
U_n(\theta)
={}&-
\int_{\mathcal D}
\left\{\int f(x)\log f(x)\lambda(dx)\right\}\Pi_n(df)\\
&+
\int_{\mathcal D}
\left\{\int f(x)\log q_\theta(x)\lambda(dx)\right\}\Pi_n(df).
\end{aligned}
$$

The first term is constant in $\theta$. Under conditions that permit the order
of integration to be exchanged, maximizing $U_n$ is equivalent to maximizing

$$
\widetilde U_n(\theta)
=\int_{\mathcal X}\log q_\theta(x)P_n^{\mathrm{pred}}(dx).
\tag{10}
$$

Read (10) as the average log score of action $q_\theta$ under current posterior
predictive beliefs about a future observation.

The qualification about exchanging integrals refers to Tonelli/Fubini
conditions, summarized in the
[integration prerequisite](../Measure_Theory/lebesgue-measure-integration-and-densities.qmd#when-two-integrals-appear).

## A direction-of-KL issue in the printed chapter

On page 26, Walker first prints $u(f,\theta)=-d(q_\theta,f)$ and defines
$d(g,f)=\int g\log(g/f)$. The next displayed result, however, is (10), which
follows from $D_{\mathrm{KL}}(f\|q_\theta)$ as written in (8), not from the
reverse divergence. The subsequent derivation fixes the intended orientation.

# 11. Why the Bayesian bootstrap yields maximum likelihood {#walker-bootstrap}

**Optional companion excerpts.** Read
[The bootstrap random object](bayes-boots.qmd#bootstrap-random-object) and
[Walker's decision calculation](bayes-boots.qmd#bootstrap-walker-decision) for
the full weighted-distribution argument. Read
[Bayesian bootstrap in Dirac notation](../Measure_Theory/dirac-measure-and-dirac-delta.qmd#dirac-bayesian-bootstrap)
only if $\sum_iW_i\delta_{X_i}$ is unfamiliar.

Under the Bayesian bootstrap, a posterior draw is

$$
F^{(b)}=\sum_{i=1}^nW_i^{(b)}\delta_{X_i},
\qquad
W^{(b)}\sim\operatorname{Dirichlet}(1,\ldots,1).
$$

Its posterior mean is the empirical distribution

$$
\widehat F_n=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\delta_{X_i}.
$$

Substituting the posterior predictive mean into (10),

$$
\widetilde U_n(\theta)
=\int\log q_\theta(x)\widehat F_n(dx)
=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\log q_\theta(X_i).
$$

Therefore the Bayes action under this utility is the maximum likelihood
estimator.

This is not a statement that the empirical distribution has a Lebesgue
density. It is a discrete probability measure, and the integral is a finite
sum.

## A distribution over projected actions

Instead of maximizing posterior **expected** utility once, project each
posterior draw:

$$
\theta^{(b)}
=\arg\max_\theta
\sum_{i=1}^nW_i^{(b)}\log q_\theta(X_i).
\tag{11}
$$

Repeated Dirichlet weights induce a distribution over $\theta^{(b)}$. Walker
connects (11) with the weighted likelihood bootstrap
[@newton1994weighted]. This distribution is not the same object as the single
Bayes action that maximizes expected utility.

# 12. Why Walker studies asymptotics {#walker-asymptotics}

**Optional companion excerpt.**
[The two probability laws](../Measure_Theory/posterior-consistency.qmd#consistency-two-laws)
separates the Bayesian prior-predictive law from the repeated-sampling law at
a fixed $f_0$. That distinction is the only prerequisite needed for Walker's
discussion of Doob's theorem.

The prior performs two tasks:

1. it represents initial uncertainty about the sampling distribution;
2. together with Bayes' rule, it determines how learning proceeds as data
   accumulate.

Asymptotic analysis evaluates the second task.

## Bayesian joint model versus fixed truth

Inside the Bayesian model,

$$
m_n(x_{1:n})
=\int\prod_{i=1}^nf(x_i)\Pi(df)
$$

is the marginal law of the observations.

For repeated-sampling evaluation, instead fix $f_0$ and suppose

$$
X_1,X_2,\ldots\overset{\mathrm{iid}}\sim f_0.
$$

These are not contradictory statements. The first specifies the Bayesian
learning model; the second evaluates that learning rule under a fixed
data-generating mechanism. We need not assume that Nature sampled $f_0$ from
$\Pi$.

## Where Doob's theorem fits

Walker mentions Doob's consistency theorem in this discussion. In simplified
terms, under appropriate identifiability and measurability conditions, Doob's
result provides a set of parameter or density values having prior probability
one at which the posterior is consistent [@doob1949application]. This is a
**prior-almost-everywhere** conclusion; it is not a guarantee for every
preselected fixed truth $f_0$, and it does not provide a contraction rate.

That distinction matters in an infinite-dimensional model. A particular
scientifically relevant $f_0$ could lie in the prior-null exceptional set, so
fixed-truth consistency theorems ask directly for conditions that work at the
chosen $f_0$.

The prior-predictive law $m_n$ is still a mathematically valid marginal law
inside the Bayesian hierarchy. Walker's criticism is better read as a warning
that this internally specified law need not be accepted as the literal
external mechanism that generated repeated datasets. The Bayesian model law
and the fixed-truth evaluation law answer different questions.

# 13. Posterior consistency {#walker-consistency}

**Optional companion excerpts.** Use
[the general consistency statement](../Measure_Theory/posterior-consistency.qmd#consistency-statement)
to decode the limit, [Reading Walker's display](../Measure_Theory/posterior-consistency.qmd#consistency-walker-display)
for a line-by-line reading, and
[Support is not the whole theorem](../Measure_Theory/posterior-consistency.qmd#support-is-important-but-not-the-whole-theorem)
only for the roles of tests, sieves, and entropy.

For a distance $d$ and every $\varepsilon>0$, consistency at $f_0$ means

$$
\boxed{
\Pi\{f:d(f,f_0)>\varepsilon\mid X_{1:n}\}
\longrightarrow0
\quad P_0^\infty\text{-almost surely}.
}
\tag{12}
$$

The probability law $P_0^\infty$ governs the infinite iid data sequence. The
quantity on the left is random because it is a function of the observed data.

The symbol $P_0^\infty$ and “almost surely” are expanded in
[the two-probability-laws section](../Measure_Theory/posterior-consistency.qmd#consistency-two-laws).

Walker emphasizes Hellinger distance. One common convention is

$$
h^2(f_0,f)
=\frac12\int\{\sqrt{f_0(x)}-\sqrt{f(x)}\}^2\lambda(dx).
$$

Constants differ across authors and do not change the topology.

Consistency theorems typically combine

- positive prior mass near $f_0$, often in KL neighborhoods;
- tests separating $f_0$ from alternatives;
- complexity or sieve control so overly rich parts of the model receive
  sufficiently little effective mass.

Tests, sieves, entropy, topology, and support are proof-level terms explained
in plain language in the [posterior-consistency note](../Measure_Theory/posterior-consistency.qmd#support-is-important-but-not-the-whole-theorem).

Having broad or even full topological support is not, by itself, a universal
consistency proof. The targeted explanation is
[Support is important but not the whole theorem](../Measure_Theory/posterior-consistency.qmd#support-is-important-but-not-the-whole-theorem).

# 14. General posterior inference from loss plus KL {#walker-loss-kl}

**Optional companion excerpt.**
[KL between belief distributions](../Other/km-divergence.qmd#kl-belief-distributions)
explains why KL is now comparing a candidate posterior $\mu$ with the prior
$\Pi$, rather than comparing two data-generating distributions.

Walker's Section 1.5 is one of the chapter's most important ideas. Instead of
starting from Bayes' theorem, he asks which probability measure $\mu$ on
$\mathcal D$ should represent posterior beliefs after observing data.

The optimization variable is therefore an entire candidate belief
distribution $\mu$, not a finite parameter vector. Problems of this type are
often called **variational** problems.

## Loss to the data

Use self-information loss for a candidate density:

$$
\ell(f,x)=-\log f(x).
$$

If beliefs about $f$ are represented by $\mu$, expected cumulative data loss is

$$
-\int_{\mathcal D}\log L_n(f)\mu(df)
=-\sum_{i=1}^n\int_{\mathcal D}\log f(X_i)\mu(df).
$$

## Loss from departing from prior information

Penalize departure from the prior by

$$
D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\mu\|\Pi)
=\int\log\left(\frac{d\mu}{d\Pi}(f)\right)\mu(df),
$$

with value $+\infty$ if $\mu\not\ll\Pi$.

## The optimization problem

Choose $\mu$ to minimize

$$
\mathcal J_n(\mu)
=-\int\log L_n(f)\mu(df)
+D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\mu\|\Pi).
\tag{13}
$$

Let the ordinary posterior satisfy

$$
\frac{d\Pi_n}{d\Pi}(f)=\frac{L_n(f)}{m_n}.
$$

Then

$$
\begin{aligned}
D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\mu\|\Pi_n)
&=\int\log\left(
\frac{d\mu/d\Pi}{d\Pi_n/d\Pi}
\right)d\mu\\
&=D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\mu\|\Pi)
-\int\log L_n(f)\mu(df)
+\log m_n.
\end{aligned}
$$

Hence

$$
\mathcal J_n(\mu)
=D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\mu\|\Pi_n)-\log m_n.
$$

Because KL is minimized at zero,

$$
\arg\min_\mu\mathcal J_n(\mu)=\Pi_n.
\tag{14}
$$

The ordinary Bayesian posterior is therefore the distribution that optimally
balances cumulative log loss against KL departure from the prior. This idea was
later developed into a broader framework for updating with general losses
[@bissiri2016general].

# 15. Fractional or power posteriors {#walker-fractional}

**Optional companion excerpt.**
[Fractional or power posteriors](../Measure_Theory/posterior-consistency.qmd#consistency-fractional-posteriors)
explains the interpretation of the powered likelihood and the limits of the
associated consistency claim. The calculation below records Walker's more
specific rate argument.

Walker allows a data-weight $\alpha_n\geq0$ in (13):

$$
\mathcal J_{n,\alpha_n}(\mu)
=-\alpha_n\int\log L_n(f)\mu(df)
+D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\mu\|\Pi).
$$

The same calculation gives

$$
\Pi_{n,\alpha_n}(df)
=\frac{L_n(f)^{\alpha_n}\Pi(df)}
{\int L_n(g)^{\alpha_n}\Pi(dg)}.
\tag{15}
$$

Special cases are

- $\alpha_n=0$: no update, so $\Pi_{n,0}=\Pi$;
- $\alpha_n=1$: ordinary Bayes;
- $0<\alpha_n<1$: a fractional or tempered posterior.

A fractional posterior stays closer to the prior by downweighting the data.
Walker discusses consistency results for such learning rules
[@walker2001consistency]. These are conditional mathematical results, not a
claim that every choice $\alpha<1$ fixes every inconsistency.

## Map of Walker's final consistency calculation

The chapter's last technical argument can be read without reproducing every
bound. Define the likelihood ratio

$$
R_n(f)=\prod_{i=1}^n\frac{f(X_i)}{f_0(X_i)}
$$

and an alternative set

$$
A_\varepsilon=\{f:h(f_0,f)>\varepsilon\}.
$$

Then the fractional posterior probability is a numerator-to-denominator ratio:

$$
\Pi_{n,\alpha_n}(A_\varepsilon)
=\frac{\int_{A_\varepsilon}R_n(f)^{\alpha_n}\Pi(df)}
{\int R_n(f)^{\alpha_n}\Pi(df)}.
\tag{16}
$$

Walker proceeds in two directions:

1. **Lower-bound the denominator.** Prior concentration near $f_0$ supplies a
   rate $\varepsilon_n$ and a bound related to
   $\int R_n(f)^{1/2}\Pi(df)$.
2. **Upper-bound the numerator.** Hellinger separation on
   $A_\varepsilon$ makes the expected numerator decay at a rate involving
   $n(1-\alpha_n)\varepsilon^2$.

Balancing the bounds leads to a condition of the form

$$
n\left\{(1-\alpha_n)\varepsilon^2
-4c\varepsilon_n^2\alpha_n\right\}\longrightarrow\infty.
$$

One admissible form is

$$
\alpha_n=1-\psi_n\varepsilon_n^2,
$$

where $\psi_n\to\infty$ but
$\psi_n\varepsilon_n^2\to0$. Thus the learning rule can approach ordinary
Bayes while retaining the stated consistency control. The example in the
chapter takes $\varepsilon_n^2=(\log n)/n$ and $\psi_n=\log n$, giving

$$
\alpha_n=1-\frac{(\log n)^2}{n}.
$$

# 16. Mathematical structure and Walker's viewpoint {#walker-structure-viewpoint}

| Claim | Status |
|---|---|
| A prior on a parameter induces a prior on sampling distributions | Mathematical fact |
| Conditional iid mixtures are exchangeable | Mathematical fact |
| $\Pi(df)$ is measure-integration notation | Mathematical fact |
| The posterior has RN derivative proportional to likelihood | Mathematical fact, under normalizing and measurability conditions |
| KL projection leads to posterior-predictive expected log score | Mathematical fact with the orientation in (8) |
| Bayesian bootstrap posterior mean yields the MLE decision | Mathematical fact for this setup |
| A Bayesian prior should be “complete” enough that it is never checked | Walker's normative position |
| Post-data selection makes the resulting posterior meaningless as belief | Walker's normative critique of an unmodeled workflow |
| BNP is generally preferable whenever parametric shape is uncertain | Modeling recommendation, not theorem |
| Ordinary Bayes need not be nonparametrically consistent | Mathematical fact; consistency needs conditions |
| The specific fractional posterior is consistent under stated conditions | Theorem-level claim with assumptions |

# 17. Corrections to tempting slogans

## “Let the data speak for themselves”

No model does this literally. A BNP prior determines support, smoothness,
tail behavior, clustering, and learning rate. The data speak through those
assumptions.

## “A DP spreads mass over every possible shape”

A DP draw is discrete. A DP mixture induces a flexible but still constrained
class of densities determined by its kernel and base measure.

## “Nonparametric means infinitely many parameters must all be learned”

Inference usually targets a distribution, function, prediction, or functional,
with regularization supplied by the prior. Finite data occupy only finite
portions of many infinite representations.

## “A misspecified parametric posterior can never learn anything”

It can learn a KL-best approximation or useful functionals under conditions.
The limitation is that it cannot leave its support and may give misleading
uncertainty if its scientific approximation is poor.

## “A broad prior guarantees consistency”

Support is necessary in the relevant sense, but infinite-dimensional
consistency also requires control of testing and complexity.

# 18. A compact reading of the chapter

Walker's chapter can now be reduced to one sequence:

1. Put a probability law $\Pi$ on candidate sampling distributions.
2. Conditional iid sampling produces an exchangeable learning model.
3. Update $\Pi$ through the likelihood to obtain $\Pi_n$.
4. Average under $\Pi_n$ to predict future data.
5. If a low-dimensional answer is required, obtain it as a posterior decision
   rather than pretending the full distribution was parametric.
6. Study consistency because the prior specifies not only initial beliefs but
   the learning dynamics.
7. View Bayes as the minimizer of data loss plus KL departure from prior.
8. Changing the relative weight of those two terms gives fractional learning
   rules.

# 19. Symbol glossary

| Symbol | Read it as |
|---|---|
| $\mathcal D$ | Space of candidate densities |
| $\Pi(df)$ | Prior measure on that space |
| $\Pi_n(df)$ | Posterior measure after $n$ observations |
| $L_n(f)$ | Likelihood at candidate density $f$ |
| $m_n$ | Integral of likelihood under the prior |
| $d\Pi_n/d\Pi$ | Posterior density relative to prior |
| $P_n^{\mathrm{pred}}$ | Posterior predictive probability measure |
| $f_n$ | Predictive density when it exists |
| $f_0$ | Fixed true density for asymptotic evaluation |
| $P_0^\infty$ | Infinite-product sampling law under $f_0$ |
| $\mu$ | Candidate belief distribution in the variational problem |
| $\alpha_n$ | Relative weight on cumulative log likelihood |

# 20. Check your understanding

Select each **Answer** box after working out the question yourself.

**1. What are the domain and codomain of the prior $\Pi$?**

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answer

Formally,

$$
\Pi:\mathscr G\longrightarrow[0,1],
$$

where $\mathscr G$ is the sigma-field of measurable subsets of the candidate
density space $\mathcal D$. Thus $\Pi$ takes a measurable **set of entire
densities** as input and returns its prior probability. Saying informally that
“$\Pi$ is on $\mathcal D$” means that $(\mathcal D,\mathscr G)$ is its
underlying measurable space.
:::

**2. Why are the observations dependent marginally but iid conditionally?**

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answer

Given one shared density $f$, the model specifies

$$
P(X_1\in A_1,\ldots,X_n\in A_n\mid f)
=\prod_{i=1}^nP_f(A_i),
$$

so the observations are conditionally iid. Marginally, $f$ is integrated out.
All observations then share the same unresolved random $f$, so learning from
one observation changes beliefs relevant to the others and generally induces
dependence.
:::

**3. Write the posterior probability of a measurable set
$A\subseteq\mathcal D$.**

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answer

Provided $0<m_n(x_{1:n})<\infty$,

$$
\Pi_n(A)
=\Pi(A\mid x_{1:n})
=\frac{\int_A\prod_{i=1}^nf(x_i)\Pi(df)}
{\int_{\mathcal D}\prod_{i=1}^ng(x_i)\Pi(dg)}.
$$

The different dummy letter $g$ in the denominator emphasizes that it ranges
over every candidate density.
:::

**4. What is the difference between $\Pi_n$ and
$P_n^{\mathrm{pred}}$?**

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answer

$\Pi_n$ is the posterior probability measure on **model space**; it assigns
probability to sets of candidate densities $f$. The posterior predictive
$P_n^{\mathrm{pred}}$ is a probability measure on **data space**; it assigns
probability to possible future observations and is obtained by averaging:

$$
P_n^{\mathrm{pred}}(B)=\int_{\mathcal D}P_f(B)\Pi_n(df).
$$
:::

**5. Which orientation of KL produces the expected log score in (10)?**

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answer

The required orientation is
$D_{\mathrm{KL}}(f\|q_\theta)$, with the unknown candidate density first and
the action density second. After averaging its negative under $\Pi_n$, the term
that depends on $\theta$ is

$$
\int\log q_\theta(x)P_n^{\mathrm{pred}}(dx).
$$
:::

**6. Why is the empirical distribution in the Bayesian-bootstrap calculation a
measure rather than a Lebesgue density?**

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answer

The empirical distribution is

$$
\widehat F_n=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\delta_{X_i},
$$

a probability measure with atoms at the observations. A finite set has
Lebesgue measure zero but receives total $\widehat F_n$-mass one, so
$\widehat F_n\not\ll\lambda$ and it has no ordinary Lebesgue density.
:::

**7. Under which law is the almost-sure convergence in (12) evaluated?**

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answer

Under $P_0^\infty$, the infinite-product sampling law for an iid sequence from
the fixed true density $f_0$. The exceptional set consists of infinite data
sequences and must have $P_0^\infty$-probability zero; the statement is not
evaluated under the prior $\Pi$.
:::

**8. Why does minimizing (13) give the ordinary posterior?**

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answer

Bayes' rule lets the objective be rewritten as

$$
\mathcal J_n(\mu)
=D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\mu\|\Pi_n)-\log m_n.
$$

The second term is constant in $\mu$, and KL divergence is nonnegative with
minimum zero at $\mu=\Pi_n$ (up to equality as probability measures). Hence the
unique minimizer under the stated conditions is the ordinary posterior.
:::

**9. Which parts of Walker's “complete prior” argument are philosophical rather
than measure-theoretic?**

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answer

Measure theory establishes that a prior is a probability measure on model
space, that a parametric prior induces such a measure, and that Bayes' rule
reweights it by the likelihood. It does **not** prove the normative claims that
an analyst must encode every acknowledged form of model uncertainty in one
pre-data “complete” prior, that unmodeled post-data model selection cannot be
interpreted as coherent personal belief, or that BNP is generally preferable
whenever parametric shape is uncertain. Those are Walker's philosophical and
workflow recommendations; their force depends on the intended interpretation
of Bayesian inference.
:::

**10. What does Doob's theorem fail to guarantee about a particular fixed
truth $f_0$?**

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answer

Its classical Bayesian consistency conclusion is prior-almost-everywhere: it
can exclude a set of possible truths having prior probability zero. It
therefore does not by itself guarantee consistency at every particular
scientifically chosen $f_0$, and it does not state how quickly the posterior
contracts. Fixed-truth consistency analysis supplies conditions directed at
that named $f_0$.
:::
